opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it's really about staying calibrated. I spend most of my time working remotely, and you can follow everything online: the papers, the Twitter discourse, the model releases. But there's a whole layer of information that never makes it onto the internet. It's what people are excited about over dinner, which research directions labs are quietly betting on, and what the vibe is around things like scaling or reinforcement learning or open models. You only pick that up by being in the room.

The Bay Area is still the center of gravity for AI. The density of people working on frontier models there is unlike anywhere else. When I come back, I have a dozen conversations in a few days, and each one updates my priors a little. Sometimes I realize something I thought was niche is actually what everyone's working on. Other times I see that the public narrative is way ahead of, or way behind, what's actually happening inside the labs.

There's also a human side to it. A lot of my work, especially around open models and post-training, depends on relationships and trust. Seeing people in person keeps those connections real, so it isn't just reply threads. And honestly, it's energizing. You leave with a bunch of new ideas and a clearer sense of what matters, and then you go home and actually have the quiet time to write and build on them. That balance works really well for me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says returning to the Bay Area helps them stay calibrated and learn what is happening inside labs and among researchers—information they say is only picked up by being there in person.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'm based in Seattle now with AI2, and I love it there, but I try to get down to the Bay a few times a year, and honestly it's less about any single meeting and more about calibration. So much of what's actually happening in AI doesn't show up in papers or blog posts for months, if ever. It lives in conversations. Somebody at a dinner mentions what's working in their post-training stack, or what isn't, or that a lab has quietly shifted its priorities, and that's the stuff that tells you where the field is really going, as opposed to where the press releases say it's going.

And there's a density thing. In Seattle I can talk to great people, but in the Bay you can have five of those conversations in a day, across labs that are supposedly competitors, and you start to see the pattern. For me, writing Interconnects, that's enormously valuable. A lot of my job is basically triangulation, and you can't triangulate from one data point.

The other piece is that the culture is genuinely different. Being around people who think the thing they're building is going to change everything, even when I disagree with them, it recalibrates how ambitious I'm being. You can get a little comfortable working at a nonprofit doing open models, and then you go down there and you remember how fast everyone else is moving, and it's a useful jolt. I wouldn't want to live inside that bubble full time, because I think some perspective comes from being outside it, but I'd be worse at my job if I never stepped back into it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he visits the Bay a few times a year for calibration, explaining that important AI developments surface in conversations before they appear in papers or posts. He says those conversations reveal where the field is really going.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of context you pick up just by being there and talking to people. You get a sense of what people are excited about, what they’re struggling with, and which ideas they’re actually taking seriously. That’s much harder to get from reading papers or following conversations online.

But I also think it’s useful to step away. The Bay Area has a very strong shared perspective on AI, and when you’re immersed in it, that can start to feel like the only perspective. Coming back regularly lets you stay connected, while having some distance gives you room to think independently.

r001.rationale: The response says being there provides firsthand context about what people are excited about, struggling with, and taking seriously, and that coming back regularly keeps you connected. It also says this is harder to learn remotely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of context you get from being there in person that’s hard to pick up remotely. You can read the papers and follow the announcements, but talking to people helps you understand what they’re excited about, what’s actually working, and where they’re running into problems. In AI, those things change so quickly that your picture can get stale pretty fast.

At the same time, I like having some distance from the Bay Area. It’s easy for everyone’s assumptions to start reinforcing one another. Going back regularly lets you reconnect and challenge your understanding, then step away and think about what you actually believe.

r001.rationale: The response says in-person context is hard to get remotely, that AI changes quickly enough for one’s picture to become stale, and that returning regularly helps reconnect and update one’s understanding of what is happening.
